q: Maria was born in 1965 and her full retirement age is 67. She claims her Social Security retirement benefit at 62. Her primary insurance amount (PIA) is $2,000 per month. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: She receives nothing until full retirement age, so claiming at 62 is not possible
She receives $2,000 per month, because the claiming age does not affect the benefit
She receives a permanently reduced benefit, because claiming before full retirement age reduces benefits, with the reduction depending on how many months early she claims
She receives $2,000 per month until 67, then a higher amount, because early claiming increases the benefit
rationale: Wrong — benefits can be claimed as early as age 62, subject to the reduction.
Wrong — the claiming age has a direct effect on the monthly amount, so $2,000 is only the amount at full retirement age.
Correct — claiming before FRA permanently reduces the benefit, based on the months before FRA.
Wrong — early claiming reduces the benefit, and it is not restored at 67.
explanation: Claiming at 62 for FRA 67 reduces the benefit to about 70% of PIA. The reduction is permanent (aside from limited situations).

q: A client's full retirement age is 67. He delays claiming until 70 and his PIA is $2,400 per month. Which statement about his benefit is most accurate?
choices: His benefit decreases after full retirement age, because the credits expire
His benefit at 70 is the same as at 62, because the increase is capped at full retirement age
His benefit is $2,400 per month, because delaying past full retirement age has no effect
His benefit increases by delayed retirement credits for each month after full retirement age, up to age 70, so the benefit at 70 is higher than the PIA
rationale: Wrong — delayed retirement credits do not expire; they increase the benefit while he delays.
Wrong — the benefit at 62 is reduced, so it is lower, not the same as at 70.
Wrong — delaying past full retirement age earns delayed retirement credits, which increase the benefit.
Correct — delayed retirement credits accrue for each month between FRA and age 70, so the benefit is higher than the PIA at 70.
explanation: Delayed retirement credits increase the benefit for each year claimed after FRA, up to age 70, with no further gain beyond that age.

q: A 63-year-old client is still working and has not reached full retirement age. He claims Social Security and earns more than the annual earnings limit for that year. Which statement is correct?
choices: His benefits are reduced by $1 for every $2 of earnings above the limit
His benefits are not affected, because the earnings test applies only after full retirement age
His benefits are permanently forfeited, regardless of later earnings
His benefits are reduced by $1 for every $1 of earnings above the limit
rationale: Correct — $1 is withheld for every $2 of earnings above the annual limit before full retirement age.
Wrong — the earnings test applies before full retirement age, which is exactly when he is subject to it.
Wrong — withheld amounts are recalculated, and benefits are increased at FRA; they are not forfeited.
Wrong — the earnings test is $1 withheld for every $2 above the limit, not $1 for every $1.
explanation: Before FRA, $1 of benefits is withheld for every $2 of earnings above the annual limit. In the year of FRA, a higher threshold applies, with a $1-for-$3 reduction.

q: A retired couple files jointly and has provisional income of $40,000. Their Social Security benefits total $30,000. Which statement is most accurate about taxation of Social Security?
choices: None of their benefits are taxable, because they are under $100,000 of income
Up to 50% of their benefits may be taxable, because provisional income is above the joint base amount but below the upper threshold
Up to 85% of their benefits may be taxable, because provisional income is above the upper threshold
All of their benefits are taxable, because they are married filing jointly
rationale: Wrong — the thresholds are based on provisional income, not total income, and they are $32,000 base and $44,000 upper for joint filers.
Correct — with provisional income between the base and upper thresholds, up to 50% of benefits can be taxable.
Wrong — 85% applies only above the upper threshold, which this couple has not crossed at $40,000.
Wrong — taxation is capped at 85%, and it depends on provisional income.
explanation: Provisional income = AGI (excluding SS) + tax-exempt interest + 50% of SS. Joint thresholds are $32,000 and $44,000; single thresholds are $25,000 and $34,000. These thresholds are not indexed.

q: A married participant in a defined benefit plan is choosing between a single-life annuity and a joint and survivor annuity. Under federal rules, which statement is correct?
choices: The spouse automatically receives 100% of the pension after retirement, regardless of election
Only the participant's employer decides which option applies
The spouse must consent in writing if the participant elects an option that does not provide a survivor benefit
The participant may choose any option without spousal involvement
rationale: Wrong — the survivor benefit is a choice that depends on the option elected, not an automatic 100% benefit.
Wrong — the participant, with spousal consent where required, makes the election, not the employer.
Correct — qualified plans generally require the spouse's written, notarized (or witnessed) consent to waive the qualified joint and survivor annuity.
Wrong — federal rules generally require spousal consent to waive the survivor annuity, so the participant cannot choose freely.
explanation: Under ERISA, the qualified joint and survivor annuity is the default for married participants. Waiving it requires notarized or witnessed spousal consent.

q: A client born in 1958 turned 73 this year. She is retired and her traditional IRA had a balance of $500,000 on December 31 of last year. Which statement about her first RMD is most accurate?
choices: Her RMD is based on the current year-end balance, so she cannot calculate it until December 31
Her first RMD is due by December 31 of this year, based on the prior year-end balance and her life expectancy factor
Her first RMD is not due until age 75 under current law
Her first RMD is due by April 1 of next year, computed from the prior year-end balance and the Uniform Lifetime Table; taking it then means two RMDs in that year
rationale: Wrong — the calculation uses the prior year-end balance, not the current year-end balance.
Wrong — the first RMD is not due by December 31 of the year she reaches the age; that deadline applies to later years, and the first one may be delayed to April 1.
Wrong — age 75 applies only to people born in 1960 or later; she was born in 1958, so the RMD age is 73.
Correct — the first RMD may be taken by April 1 of the following year, using the prior year-end balance and the Uniform Lifetime Table. Delaying it means two distributions fall in that year.
explanation: RMD age is 73 for those born 1951 to 1959 and 75 for those born 1960 or later. The first RMD can be delayed to April 1 of the following year, which means two RMDs in that year.

q: A non-spouse adult child inherits a traditional IRA from a parent who died in 2026 after reaching RMD age. The child is not disabled, chronically ill, or a minor. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The child must fully distribute the account by the end of the tenth year after death, and annual distributions are required during that period if the parent had started RMDs
The child is not required to take any distributions, because the account is inherited
The child must distribute the account within five years, regardless of the parent's RMD status
The child can stretch distributions over her own life expectancy
rationale: Correct — under the 10-year rule, the account is depleted by year 10, and annual RMDs apply when the owner had already begun RMDs.
Wrong — the account is subject to distribution rules, and an inherited traditional IRA is not exempt from them.
Wrong — the five-year rule applies in some cases where the owner died before RMDs began, not in this situation.
Wrong — life-expectancy stretch is available only to eligible designated beneficiaries, which this child is not.
explanation: Non-eligible designated beneficiaries: 10-year rule. If the owner died after the RMD start, annual distributions must continue in years 1 through 9 as well.

q: A client, age 57, opened a Roth IRA 3 years ago with a $30,000 contribution. He wants to withdraw the full $30,000 now for a home purchase. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: He may withdraw the earnings tax-free but must pay tax on the contributions
He may withdraw the contributions at any time, tax-free and penalty-free, because contributions to a Roth IRA are always accessible
He may not withdraw anything, because the five-year rule blocks all distributions for 5 years
He must pay tax and a 10% penalty on the full amount
rationale: Wrong — contributions come out first and are not taxed; earnings are the portion subject to tests.
Correct — Roth IRA contributions can be withdrawn at any time, free of tax and penalty, because they were made with after-tax dollars.
Wrong — the five-year rule applies to earnings and certain conversions, not to the return of contributions.
Wrong — contributions are returned first, so the full amount is not taxable or penalized.
explanation: Roth IRA ordering: contributions come out first, tax- and penalty-free. Earnings are subject to the five-year rule and age 59½ tests.

q: A client leaves his employer at age 56. He has a 401(k) and wants to access the money without the 10% additional tax. Which statement is correct?
choices: He must wait until 59½ to avoid the 10% additional tax from any source
The exception applies only if he rolls the 401(k) to an IRA first
The rule of 55 exception allows penalty-free withdrawals from the employer plan, but only if he separated from service in or after the year he turned 55
The exception applies only to IRAs, not 401(k)s
rationale: Wrong — the rule of 55 is an exception to the 10% penalty and avoids the wait for 59½ in the employer plan.
Wrong — rolling to an IRA removes the exception, because IRA distributions do not use the separation-from-service rule.
Correct — the separation-from-service exception allows penalty-free distributions from the employer plan if he leaves in or after the year he reaches 55.
Wrong — the rule applies to employer plans like 401(k)s; it does not apply to IRAs, which is the reverse of this option.
explanation: Rule of 55: if you separate from service in or after the year you turn 55, distributions from that employer's plan are exempt from the 10% penalty. Rolling to an IRA can cause the loss of this exception.

q: A client plans to retire with a $1,000,000 portfolio. Early in retirement the market falls 25%, and he withdraws the same inflation-adjusted amount each year. Which risk does this best illustrate?
choices: Inflation risk
Reinvestment risk
Longevity risk
Sequence-of-returns risk
rationale: Wrong — inflation risk concerns purchasing power, not the timing of market losses relative to withdrawals.
Wrong — reinvestment risk is about reinvesting cash flows at lower rates, not about early losses with withdrawals.
Wrong — longevity risk is the risk of outliving assets; this scenario is about the timing of losses early in retirement.
Correct — poor returns early in retirement, combined with withdrawals, can deplete the portfolio faster than average returns would suggest.
explanation: Sequence-of-returns risk: early losses combined with withdrawals permanently impair the portfolio, even if later returns average out.

q: A client asks whether the traditional 4% withdrawal guideline is a guarantee. Which response is most accurate?
choices: No, it is a historical rule of thumb based on a set of past market scenarios, and results depend on market returns, inflation, and spending
Yes, if the portfolio is 60% stocks, the rule is guaranteed
No, the rule applies only to portfolios held entirely in bonds
Yes, the 4% rule guarantees that the portfolio will last 30 years in every market
rationale: Correct — the 4% rule is a rule of thumb derived from historical simulations and is sensitive to returns, inflation, fees, and spending flexibility.
Wrong — allocation does not turn the rule into a guarantee, although it affects outcomes.
Wrong — the rule was developed from balanced stock and bond portfolios, not bond-only ones.
Wrong — the rule is based on historical data and does not guarantee outcomes for every future market path.
explanation: The 4% rule is a historical planning heuristic; outcomes depend on sequence of returns, inflation, fees, and whether spending adjusts.

q: A client turns 65 this year and plans to delay Medicare Part B enrollment because he is still covered by his employer's group health plan through his own active employment. Which statement is correct?
choices: He must enroll in Part B at 65 to avoid any penalty, even while still working
He may delay Part B without penalty if he is covered by a group plan from current employment, and he has a special enrollment period when that coverage ends
He cannot delay Part B under any circumstances after age 65
He will automatically be enrolled in Part B at 67 without any action
rationale: Wrong — delaying is allowed under this specific situation without a late-enrollment penalty.
Correct — coverage from current employment with an employer of 20 or more employees generally allows a special enrollment period without a late penalty.
Wrong — delaying is allowed in the employment-coverage case, so the rule is not absolute.
Wrong — there is no automatic enrollment at 67; enrollment requires action or qualifying coverage status.
explanation: Medicare Part B late penalty: 10% per 12-month period of delay, unless delayed due to qualifying employer group coverage, with an eight-month special enrollment period after that coverage ends.

q: A client's modified adjusted gross income from two years ago was high because of a large Roth conversion. Which statement about Medicare Part B premiums is correct?
choices: IRMAA is based on the client's net worth, not income
Income-related monthly adjustment amounts (IRMAA) are based on the client's income from the current year only
IRMAA is based on income from two years prior, so a high-income year can raise premiums two years later
IRMAA does not apply to Part B premiums, only to Part D
rationale: Wrong — IRMAA is based on income, not on net worth.
Wrong — IRMAA uses income from two years earlier, not the current year.
Correct — IRMAA is calculated on MAGI from the tax return two years before the premium year, so a conversion can raise premiums later.
Wrong — IRMAA applies to both Part B and Part D premiums.
explanation: IRMAA uses MAGI from two years prior. Life-changing events such as retirement can be reported to request a reduction.

q: A client receives a lump-sum distribution from his employer's 401(k), including company stock with a cost basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $140,000. He does not roll the stock to an IRA. Which treatment of the net unrealized appreciation (NUA) is correct?
choices: The NUA is tax-free because it is company stock
The $100,000 NUA is taxed as ordinary income, and the $40,000 basis is taxed as long-term capital gain
The full $140,000 is taxable as ordinary income in the year of distribution
The $40,000 cost basis is taxed as ordinary income, and the $100,000 NUA is taxed at long-term capital gain rates when the shares are sold
rationale: Wrong — NUA is not tax-free; it is deferred and taxed as capital gain when the shares are sold.
Wrong — the classification is reversed: basis is ordinary income, and the NUA is capital gain.
Wrong — the NUA portion is not taxed as ordinary income at distribution if the stock is distributed in-kind and the rules are followed.
Correct — the cost basis is ordinary income at distribution, and the NUA is taxed as long-term gain when the stock is later sold, under the NUA rules.
explanation: NUA: the employer stock distributed in kind after a lump sum; cost basis taxed as ordinary income at distribution; the NUA is taxed as long-term capital gain on sale, regardless of holding period after distribution.

q: A client buys a nonqualified deferred annuity with $200,000 of after-tax premiums. The contract value grows to $260,000. He takes a lump-sum withdrawal of $60,000. Which statement about the tax treatment is most accurate, under the general rule for nonqualified annuities?
choices: The $60,000 is taxed as ordinary income up to the gain of $60,000, which is the earnings portion withdrawn first
The $60,000 is taxed as long-term capital gain, because annuities are capital assets
Only $20,000 is taxable, because withdrawals are divided by the ratio of basis to total value
The full $60,000 is tax-free because it is return of principal
rationale: Correct — under the last-in, first-out rule for nonqualified deferred annuities, earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income, up to the total gain of $60,000.
Wrong — annuity earnings are ordinary income, not long-term capital gain.
Wrong — the pro-rata approach applies to annuitized payments through the exclusion ratio, not to a lump-sum withdrawal under the general rule.
Wrong — under the general rule, withdrawals from a deferred annuity are income first, so the gain comes out before basis.
explanation: Nonqualified deferred annuities: LIFO for withdrawals. Earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income. Annuitized payments use the exclusion ratio instead.
